name: Elon Musk
title: The Boy Who Bet on Mars
subtitle: From a $500 video game in Pretoria to rockets, electric cars and the world's biggest fortune, and what it all cost him.
hook: In December 2008, both of Elon Musk's companies were close to death. On 23 December, NASA picked SpaceX, whose Falcon 9 rocket had ==never flown a full mission==, for up to **$1.6 billion** of space-station cargo flights. The next evening, at ==6 pm on Christmas Eve==, Tesla's rescue funding round finally closed. Musk later wrote that it was the "Last hour of last day possible", with the company three days from bankruptcy.

contact.howToReach: Musk's only personal public channel is his X account, @elonmusk, where he posts constantly and sometimes replies in public, but with an audience of about 240 million followers, do not expect a cold message to be read. Classic press routes are close to dead too: Tesla disbanded its US PR team in 2020, and X's press inbox once auto-replied to journalists with a poop emoji. What does work is going to the right team for the right reason: investor questions to Tesla Investor Relations or SpaceX's corporate secretary, media questions to SpaceX's media desk, and jobs through hiring calls Musk posts himself, such as the August 2026 request for a résumé plus three bullet points of exceptional ability sent to datacenters@spacex.com. The Musk Foundation's website lists its focus areas but publishes no application process, so don't send grant pitches, and never pay a "contact finder" site or trust anyone who claims to be Musk and asks for money or crypto. Keep any message under 150 words: one line on who you are, three concrete bullets on what you have actually built, and one clear ask.

chapters.title: A Boy Who Went Into His Head

blocks.text: Elon Reeve Musk was born on ==28 June 1971== in Pretoria, South Africa. He was the first of three children. His brother Kimbal came about a year later, and his sister Tosca was born in 1974.

His mother, Maye, was born in Regina, Canada, in 1948, one of twin girls. She was a dietitian and a model. She married Errol Musk, an engineer, in 1970, when she was 22, and Elon arrived about nine months later.

Errol was a South African engineer whom a relative called a "serial entrepreneur." Elon later said his father was brilliant at engineering, and Errol was supposedly the youngest person in South Africa to get a professional engineer's qualification. That last part comes from the family, so treat it as their story, not a checked record.
Notice: both parents worked for themselves. The kids watched business up close.
The flying grandparents

To understand the Musk family, you have to meet Maye's father, Joshua Haldeman. He was a chiropractor in Regina who flew his own single-engine plane around the Canadian prairies. Local papers called his family =="the Flying Haldemans."==

Haldeman was also a political activist. By 1940 he was a leader in Technocracy Inc., a movement that wanted engineers and scientists, not politicians, to run the country. Canada banned the group that year, and Haldeman was arrested and found guilty of undermining the war effort. In 1950 he sold up and moved his family to South Africa.

CBC News, which dug through his writing, reported that he openly supported apartheid and held racist and conspiracist views. That is part of the family history too, and later writers have argued about how much it shaped the household Elon grew up in.
In Canada, they thought we were crazy because my parents would fly around in their single-prop canvas plane with their small children.
blocks.who: Maye Musk, in her 2019 book A Woman Makes a Plan

blocks.text: In South Africa the Haldemans kept exploring. For years their family holidays were long trips into the Kalahari Desert, hunting for a legendary "Lost City" that almost certainly never existed. The family also tells a story that the grandparents flew from South Africa to Australia in a single-engine plane. Every Musk, one magazine noted, can tell stories like these about their ancestors.

Haldeman died on ==13 January 1974==, when his plane crashed near power lines during what looked like an attempted emergency landing. Elon was two. But the stories stayed. His grandmother told them, with slide shows, again and again. __Elon grew up believing that risk was simply what his family did.__
My grandfather had this desire for adventure, exploration — doing crazy things.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, to biographer Ashlee Vance

blocks.text: Family stories become a child's rulebook. Which stories does your family tell?
Without sounding patronizing, it does seem that our family is different from other people. We risk more.
The boy who seemed deaf

Maye noticed early that her first child was quick. She also noticed something strange. Elon would stare into the distance and stop responding, even in the middle of a conversation. Nobody could reach him.

His parents worried he might be going deaf. They took him to doctors, who ran tests and removed his adenoids, a common fix for children's hearing problems. Nothing changed, because his hearing was fine. He was simply lost in thought.

Elon later told biographer Ashlee Vance that, as a child, the part of his brain normally used for seeing seemed to get "taken over by internal thought processes." In plain words: he could run a picture of a problem in his head, like a movie, and test ideas on it.

That habit made school harder. His parents had sent him to school early because he read so much, so he was always the youngest boy in class. His birthday, 28 June, fell almost on the last day a child could be admitted, and he was also a late bloomer.
Elon was the youngest and smallest guy in his school.
Six years old, and walking across town

When Elon was about six, his mother grounded him and said he could not go to his cousin's birthday party. He thought the punishment was unfair. So he planned to ride his bike there, and made the mistake of telling her.

Maye told him he needed a licence to ride a bike and the police might stop him. He wasn't sure that was true, but he decided to walk instead, just in case. The party was across town, about 10 to 12 miles away by his own memory. It took him around four hours.
As he got close, his mother was leaving the party with Kimbal and Tosca. She spotted him on the road. He sprinted the last two blocks to his cousin's house, climbed a tree and refused to come down.
She saw me walking down the road and freaked out.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on the walk at age six

blocks.text: Six years old. Four hours of walking. Stubbornness shows up early.
Raised by books

Elon read constantly, sometimes for ==10 hours a day==. On shopping trips he would vanish, and the family would find him sitting on the floor at the back of the nearest bookshop. When Maye brought him to dinner parties, he would hide a book under the table if the adults got boring.
I was raised by books. Books, and then my parents.

By about the fourth grade, by his own account, he had run out of books at both the school library and the neighbourhood library. So he started reading the Encyclopaedia Britannica. He became the family's walking reference book, and Tosca nicknamed him "Genius Boy."

The habit had a cost. Elon would correct people when they got facts wrong, and that did not make him friends. At school in Pretoria other kids called him "Muskrat." His favourite books, he said later, were about heroes with a mission.
The heroes of the books I read, 'The Lord of the Rings' and the 'Foundation' series, always felt a duty to save the world.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, to The New Yorker

blocks.text: Read this twice: what you read at 9 becomes what you chase at 30.
A wild, unsupervised childhood

Elon has said that for his first eight years or so he rarely saw his parents, and there was no nanny watching him closely, only a housekeeper. With Kimbal as his partner in crime, he built rockets and mixed homemade explosives.
I'm shocked that I have all my fingers.
His sister later remembered that Elon practised hypnosis on his siblings. He was not very good at it. Tosca recalled refusing when he tried to make her eat raw bacon, and he kept trying anyway.

Errol was strict in an unusual way. In a country where white families like theirs usually had servants, he made the children play a game called "America, America." During the game they had to do everything an American child would: clean the house, mow the lawn and do the chores themselves.
The divorce, and a strange choice
Maye and Errol divorced in ==1979==, when Elon was eight. Maye later described the marriage as abusive. She took the three children and worked as a single mother, and money was tight.

To pay the bills she ran her own dietitian practice, gave wellness talks and modelled. The family skipped restaurants and films. She cut the children's hair herself and did not hover over their homework. The kids even learned to forge her signature on school forms.
I wouldn't allow them to be brats, I couldn't afford that.

About two years after the divorce, Elon made a decision that shaped the next decade. He told his mother he would go and live with his father. His reason was simple and kind: Mum had three children and Dad had none.
I felt sorry for my father, because my mother had all three kids. He seemed very sad and lonely by himself.

Errol's home, in Lone Hill near Johannesburg, had more books and more money. Kimbal later moved in too. The boys went to their father's building sites and learned plumbing, bricklaying and wiring with their hands.

Elon later said that, at the time, he did not understand what kind of person his father was. He has described Errol in very harsh words, and said his father was physically violent only when Elon was very young. Errol disputes this and says he "smacked" Elon once, "on the bottom." Both versions are on the record.
It was not absent of good, but it was not a happy childhood.
Emeralds, chocolate bars and a trip to America

Errol also traded in emeralds. Kimbal remembered flying into Zambia with their father in a plane loaded with chocolate bars, because the customs officers wanted chocolate. As Kimbal put it, you handed them chocolate and they let you do business.

Errol later told reporters the family was so rich that the safe would not close. Biographer Walter Isaacson found a messier story. In 1986 Errol swapped a light plane for emeralds from a Zambian mine owned by a businessman. Errol told Isaacson the mine was never registered and that the trade was not legal, and the business later collapsed.
We had so much money at times we couldn't even close our safe.
blocks.who: Errol Musk, as quoted by The Independent

blocks.text: Myth check: Isaacson found Errol never actually owned an emerald mine.

Around the age of ten, Errol took Elon on a trip to the United States. Elon had decided it was the most exciting place on Earth, because every comic book seemed to happen there. In American hotels he discovered arcade game rooms and kept asking himself one question: how do you make these games?

Back in South Africa, Elon saw a home computer in a shop at the mall and begged his father for it. He put in his saved pocket money, and his father paid the rest. It was a ==Commodore VIC-20==, a machine with about 5 kilobytes of memory.

photo.caption: A Commodore VIC-20, the kind of home computer Elon got at about age 10. Its BASIC lessons were meant to take months. He finished them in days.
photo.author: Evan-Amos

blocks.text: The computer came with a course in the BASIC programming language. It was meant to take about six months. Elon, ten years old, barely slept and finished it in three days.
It was supposed to take like six months to get through all the lessons.

Then he did something smart. He started writing his own games and selling them so he could buy better games and better computers. __From the very start, he treated a skill as a way to pay for more learning.__

blocks.title: Turn your obsession into a loop
blocks.text: At ten, Elon did not just play games. He learned to make them, sold them and used the money to buy better tools. Pick one skill you love and find a small way to get paid for it, so the skill pays for its own growth.

chapters.title: Bullies, Blastar and a Way Out

blocks.text: In 1984 a South African computer magazine called PC and Office Technology printed a page of code signed "E. R. Musk." It was a space game called ==Blastar==. The player flies a lonely ship and has to destroy an alien freighter carrying hydrogen bombs.

The magazine paid Elon ==$500== for it. Most accounts say he was 12, though one book says 13. The game is very simple, a bit like Space Invaders. But it was written by a child, alone, in a language he had taught himself from a manual.

blocks.text: Twelve years old. First paying customer. No permission needed.
In his own telling, the money was never the point. It bought the next thing. He has said he spent his earnings on better computers and Dungeons & Dragons modules.
The years he calls the worst

School was brutal. Elon was small, young for his year and, by his father's account, quick to call other kids stupid. Isaacson's biography says he lacked the urge to win friends, which did not help. He was bullied for years.
The gangs at school would hunt me down – literally hunt me down!

Kimbal described the culture bluntly: South Africa then was rough, "rougher than that," and the bullying hit Elon hard. Tosca pointed out there was no escape. However bad it got, you still had to get up and go to school the next morning.

Around the age of 12 or 13, one fight went very wrong. At recess a boy bumped into Elon, Elon pushed back, and words were exchanged. Later the boy and his friends came for him. They pushed him down a flight of concrete steps, sat on him and kicked him in the head.
When they got finished, I couldn't even recognize his face.
blocks.who: Kimbal Musk, who was with him, to Walter Isaacson

blocks.text: Elon spent days in hospital. Decades later he still needed surgery on his nose because of that beating. But what he says hurt more came after.

Elon and Kimbal both told Isaacson that when Elon came home, their father shouted at him for an hour. Errol told Isaacson that the other boy had recently lost his father to suicide and that Elon had called him stupid. Errol denies shouting at his son at all.
I had to stand for an hour as he yelled at me and called me an idiot and told me that I was just worthless.
No, I did not berate Elon. That is nonsense.
Two people, two memories. Good biographies show both. So do we.

After the attack, Errol moved Elon out of that school. He enrolled both boys at Pretoria Boys High School, a well-known school in Pretoria, and has said he bought a house in another city to make it possible.

photo.caption: Pretoria Boys High School, where Elon finished school in 1988 after the attack at his earlier school.
photo.author: Gamtoos at English Wikipedia

blocks.text: Veldskool: a camp built on fighting

There was another ordeal. Elon was sent to a wilderness survival camp called veldskool. Isaacson writes that bullying there was considered a virtue. Children got small rations of food and water and were encouraged to fight over them.
It was so insane, mind-blowing.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on veldskool, to Walter Isaacson

blocks.text: Elon called it a "paramilitary Lord of the Flies." On his first stay he was beaten up twice and lost about ==10 pounds==, roughly four and a half kilos.
Looking for the meaning of life at 14

Between about 13 and 15, Elon hit what he calls an existential crisis. He wanted to know what life meant, and it all looked meaningless. The house happened to have books by the gloomy German philosophers Nietzsche and Schopenhauer, and he read them.
...which you should not read at age 14. It is bad, it's really negative.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on Nietzsche and Schopenhauer

blocks.text: The book that pulled him out was a comedy: Douglas Adams's The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. Elon found it far more positive, and he took a serious idea from it.
A lot of times the question is harder than the answer.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

blocks.text: He decided that if humans could understand more of the universe, they could ask better questions. So expanding human knowledge, and human civilisation, became his idea of a good life. __A lot of his later ventures make more sense once you know a 14-year-old reached this conclusion.__
Very important: he fixed his mood with a better question, not an answer.
Fighting back
Elon started learning karate, judo and wrestling. Then his body caught up: a growth spurt took him to about six feet tall by 16. He has said the bullying stopped at about 15.
He told Rolling Stone that he once knocked out the biggest bully in his school with one punch, and that boy never picked on him again.
If you're fighting a bully, you cannot appease a bully.
Teen hustles: Easter eggs and an arcade
The Musk brothers kept looking for ways to make money. Once they walked door to door at night selling Easter eggs at a huge mark-up. When customers doubted the price, Kimbal had a line ready.
You are doing this to support future capitalists.
blocks.who: Kimbal Musk, selling Easter eggs as a boy

blocks.text: For example: at about 16, Elon and Kimbal tried to open a video arcade near their high school. They had signed a lease and lined up suppliers. They were stopped because the city would not grant the permission they needed, and only then did their parents find out.
We had a lease, we had suppliers, but we were actually stopped.

Kimbal said their parents "flipped out," especially their father. The idea died. But the boys learned what real deals take: a lease, suppliers, and, as they found out the hard way, licences and an adult signature.
Failed deal at 16. Cheap lesson. Check the rules before you sign.
Planning the escape

By his mid-teens Elon was sure he did not belong in South Africa. Every exciting piece of technology he read about seemed to come from the United States, or at least North America. He tried for years to get one of his divorced parents to move there. His father once agreed, then changed his mind.
At one point I convinced my father but then he reneged, unfortunately.

There was a second reason to leave. White South African boys faced compulsory military service under the apartheid government. Elon has said he had no problem with armies in general, but did not want to serve in that one.
Serving in the South African army suppressing black people just didn't seem like a really good way to spend time.

He graduated from Pretoria Boys High School in ==1988==. Then he spotted a loophole. His mother was born in Canada, so her children could claim Canadian citizenship. Elon filled out the forms for her passport and his own, mailed them, and waited.
The wait took close to a year. In the meantime he had started college classes in South Africa. When the passport finally came, he did not hang around.
Within three weeks of getting my Canadian passport, I was in Canada.
His father did not send him off kindly. Elon remembers Errol saying he would fail. He was 17, and he took the bet.
He said rather contentiously that I'd be back in three months, that I'm never going to make it.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, recalling his father, to Rolling Stone

blocks.title: Read the rules, then use them
blocks.text: Elon's way out was not luck. He studied citizenship law, found that his mother's birthplace opened a door, and did the paperwork himself. Before you say "I can't," check the rules. Sometimes the exit is written in a form nobody bothered to read.

chapters.title: Hot Dogs, Cold Calls, Big Bets

blocks.text: Elon landed in Canada in 1989 with roughly ==$2,000==. Maye had written to her uncle in Montreal to ask if Elon could stay. No reply came before he left. From a pay phone, Elon called home collect and learned the uncle had moved to Minnesota.

So he checked into the cheapest bed in a Montreal youth hostel and made a plan. He had distant relatives he had never met in Saskatchewan, the prairie province where his mother was born. He bought a cross-country bus ticket.
Nearly 2,000 miles later he got off the bus in a small town called Swift Current. He phoned a second cousin out of the blue. The cousin picked up, Elon hitched a ride, and that night he had a bed.
Seventeen. Alone. Cold-calling relatives from a bus station. That's grit.
The one-dollar-a-day test
Next problem: money. Elon worked out the least he needed to survive. He calculated that by buying hot dogs and oranges in bulk he could eat on about ==one dollar a day==.
You can really get tired of hot dogs and oranges after a while.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, to Neil deGrasse Tyson

blocks.text: The point was not to suffer. The point was to learn that if he could live on a dollar a day, earning about thirty dollars a month would keep him alive. __Once he knew his floor was that low, failure stopped looking so scary.__
For example, do the maths yourself. At one dollar a day, a whole year of food costs about $365. At $18 an hour, the boiler-room job he took later would cover that in about 20 hours of work.
Every odd job going
Elon floated between his mother's relatives' houses and took whatever work he could find. On a cousin's farm he tended vegetables and shovelled grain. In Vancouver he swung a chainsaw cutting logs.

The best-paying job he found was cleaning the boiler room of a lumber mill, for ==$18 an hour==. He put on a hazmat suit, squeezed through a narrow tunnel and shovelled steaming sand and sludge out through the same hole, while someone on the other side loaded it into a wheelbarrow.
If you stay in there for more than thirty minutes, you get too hot and die.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on the boiler-room job

blocks.text: He chose the worst job because it paid best. Think about that.

Back in South Africa, the family began following him. Tosca, 15, put the family house up for sale while Maye was away, and sold it along with the furniture and car. Maye and Tosca rented a small apartment in Toronto, and Elon slept on their pull-out couch when he visited.
Elon went to visit my family and he never came back.
Queen's University and the first business

Once he had a little money saved, Elon enrolled at Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario. For the first time, he found people who liked talking about electric cars and space. His dorm-mate Navaid Farooq, who had also grown up abroad, became a close friend over strategy games.

Elon also started a small company, Musk Computer Consulting. He built and sold custom PCs and word processors, cheaper than shop prices. An advert in a Queen's student paper promised "STATE OF THE ART" machines and told customers to call anytime, day or evening.

Kimbal joined him at Queen's a little later. The brothers then tried something bold. They read the newspaper, wrote down the names of interesting business leaders, and phoned them up one by one to ask for lunch.
Copy this: newspaper, list of names, phone. Zero cost. Huge upside.
The cold call that worked

One of the people they reached was Peter Nicholson, a senior executive at the Bank of Nova Scotia with a background in physics. He agreed to lunch, and the brothers took a three-hour train ride to meet him. They talked about philosophy, economics and how the world works. Nicholson then offered Elon the one spot on his small team: a summer internship, at about 19.
I think it's fair to say that Elon is the only person who ever called me out of the blue and asked me for a job.

Elon was given a research job on the bank's Latin American debt, including bonds known as Brady bonds. He worked out that the bank could buy more of this debt cheaply from rival banks and, by his estimate, make billions. He pushed the idea hard. The bank's leaders, already under pressure over that debt, said no.
We could just instantly make $5 billion. Right now.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on his Scotiabank idea

blocks.text: The summer taught him something lasting. He decided banks copy each other and rarely take new ideas seriously. He also got shouted at for drinking from a coffee pot reserved for executives.
If everyone else ran off a bloody cliff, they'd run right off a cliff with them.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on the banks he saw as an intern

blocks.text: Remember this view of banks. It comes back later in his story.
Penn, physics and a party house

In ==1992==, after two years at Queen's, Elon transferred to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia on a scholarship. He finally lived in the United States. He studied physics and also business at the Wharton School.
I was concerned that if I didn't study business, I would be forced to work for someone who did study business.

photo.caption: College Hall at the University of Pennsylvania. Elon transferred here in 1992 and paid his way partly by throwing house parties.
photo.author: Smallbones

blocks.text: He still needed money. With a friend, Adeo Ressi, he rented a big ten-bedroom house and on weekends turned it into a nightclub. They blacked out the windows with garbage bags, painted the walls with glow-in-the-dark paint and charged ==$5== at the door. Sometimes more than 500 people came.
I was paying my own way through college and could make an entire month's rent in one night.
Elon stayed sober at his own parties, because someone had to run them. When Maye visited, she sat at the front door with a shoebox, collecting the money.

In class, his ideas were already big. He wrote well-received papers on ultracapacitors, a way of storing energy, and on solar power collected in space. He also wrote a business plan for scanning books into digital form, years before Google launched a similar project.
Around this time he thought about which areas would matter most to humanity's future. He landed on three. __Almost everything he later built fits inside this list he made as a student.__
The three areas were the Internet, sustainable energy, and space exploration.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on choosing what to work on

blocks.text: Two internships at once

In the summer of 1994 Elon went to Silicon Valley and worked two internships at the same time. By day he worked at Pinnacle Research Institute, on ultracapacitors that might one day power electric cars.

By night he worked at a video-game start-up called Rocket Science Games. His supervisor there, Mark Greenough, remembered him as the "disc flipper" who came in at night while the game software was rendering.

At the end of the summer, Elon and Kimbal bought an old, battered 20-year-old BMW and drove it from Silicon Valley to Philadelphia. The whole drive, they talked about one thing: the internet, and what kind of business they could build on it together.
I am younger than Elon, but we were both finishing school at the same time--because I am much smarter than him!
blocks.who: Kimbal Musk, joking about the road trip

blocks.text: Too shy for Netscape

In 1995 the internet was exploding, and the hottest company was Netscape, maker of the first popular web browser. Elon applied for a job and never heard back. He even went and stood in the company's lobby, hoping to meet someone.
I was too shy to talk to anyone.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on waiting in Netscape's lobby

blocks.text: The future billionaire was too shy to speak. Shyness is normal. Act anyway.

He had a safer plan too. Stanford University had admitted him to a graduate programme in materials science, where he could have studied energy storage. Elon worried, though, that years of research might end with a single sad finding that his idea could not work.
So you add some leaves to the tree of knowledge, and the leaf is 'Nope, it's not possible.'
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on why he hesitated over a PhD

blocks.text: He went back to Peter Nicholson, the banker, for advice. On a walk in Toronto, Nicholson told him the moment would not wait. Elon asked Stanford to let him start in January 1996 instead of September 1995. Someone in the department told him they expected him back soon.
Look Elon, the dot-com rocket is ascending.
I'll bet we'll see you in three months.
blocks.who: A Stanford department contact, as reported by Jimmy Soni

blocks.text: Elon has often said he left Stanford after two days. The reporting tells a simpler story. He deferred, and Reuters, reporting on a Washington Post investigation, said he never enrolled. Either way, he did not go back.
I'm not a born risk-taker.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, to the Pennsylvania Gazette

blocks.text: Not a risk-taker. He just made sure the risk was survivable.
The first real company

In 1995 Elon, Kimbal and a friend named Greg Kouri started a company in Palo Alto. It became ==Zip2==. The idea was new for its time: online city guides, listing local businesses on the web, which it later sold to newspapers.

How it was funded is disputed. Accounts based on Ashlee Vance's biography say Errol gave the brothers $28,000. Elon says that is false. In a 2019 post he said Zip2 started with about $2,000 from him plus his home-built PC, about $5,000 from Kimbal and about $8,000 from Kouri. He added that his father later put in about 10% of a roughly $200,000 angel round.
He was irrelevant. He paid nothing for college.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, on claims that his father funded him, to Rolling Stone

blocks.text: Money was so short that the brothers did not rent an apartment. They rented a small office, slept on the couch and showered at the YMCA. They had one computer. So the website ran during the day, and Elon wrote code at night.
The website was up during the day and I was coding at night, seven days a week, all the time.

There is one more part of this story, and it is not flattering. In 2024 The Washington Post reported that Musk briefly worked in the US without legal authorisation while building the company, because he had not enrolled at Stanford. Two former colleagues recalled him getting work authorisation around 1997.
Musk denies this. He says he was on a J-1 visa that changed into an H-1B work visa. In a 2020 podcast, quoted by the Post, he put it more loosely.
I was legally there, but I was meant to be doing student work.

So this is where the boy from Pretoria stands at 24. He has about $100,000 in student debt by his own account, a tiny office, one computer and a brother who believes in him. Everything that comes next starts in that office.
Spoiler: in 1999 this tiny company sold for about $307 million.

blocks.title: Know your floor before you jump
blocks.text: Elon tested living on a dollar a day before he took big risks. Once he knew how little he needed, quitting a safe path for a start-up felt possible. Work out your real minimum. It makes brave decisions much less frightening.

Most people know Elon Musk for two or three companies. The real list is much longer, and it is full of dead ends. There is a city-guide start-up, an online bank that lost its own name, a plan to buy old Russian missiles, a tunnel to Chicago that never got dug, a political party that lasted about six weeks, and a seat at the table of an AI lab he later sued. This chapter goes through every one of them, wins and losses, in the order they happened.

Read it like a balance sheet. Each venture below shows the problem it tried to solve, why he picked it, where the first money came from, and what really happened. __The pattern that matters is not that he never failed. It is that each exit paid for the next, bigger bet.__
Watch how money from one company funds the next one.

blocks.name: Zip2
blocks.idea: In the mid-1990s, newspapers had no idea how to go online. Zip2 wrote software that helped them put listings, maps and city guides on the web. Think of it as an early, newspaper-branded version of a local search and maps app.
blocks.decision: Zip2 chose to sell to newspapers instead of going directly to readers. That meant big, slow customers, but also customers who already had local ads and trusted brands. In 1998 it nearly merged with its rival CitySearch. The deal was cancelled after about three weeks of checking each other's books, because the two sides could not agree on strategy or technology.
blocks.howStarted: Musk started it in 1995 with his brother Kimbal and their partner Greg Kouri. Tesla's later filings list Kimbal as Zip2's co-founder from November 1995. By 1998 Zip2 had about 160 partners, mostly newspaper companies, and its investors included the New York Times Co., Knight Ridder and Hearst.
blocks.funding: The very first money was tiny and came from the founders themselves (accounts of the exact amounts differ). The big cheque came in 1996 from the venture firm Mohr Davidow Ventures. Forbes reported in 2003 that it put in $3.6 million for majority control; later reporting says about $3 million. A 2024 Washington Post report, covered by Forbes, said the deal required the brothers to sort out their US work status within weeks; Musk denies he ever worked illegally.
blocks.whatHappened: Compaq bought Zip2 in early 1999 for $307 million in cash, to plug it into its AltaVista search engine. Compaq's own filing puts the total cost at $340.9 million once stock options were included. Musk was 27. His 7% stake earned him about $22 million.
blocks.lesson: Selling to businesses that already have customers can be faster than winning millions of users one by one. But giving up majority control for your first big cheque means you may not run the company you started.

blocks.text: Twenty-two million dollars at 27. He put it straight back to work.

Most people would have stopped there. Musk did the opposite. Almost straight away he put a large part of the Zip2 money into a new company that wanted to replace banks. It was a far riskier idea, in a far more regulated industry.

blocks.name: X.com, which became PayPal
blocks.idea: X.com started in March 1999 as an internet bank: one website for your savings, payments and investments. The most popular feature turned out to be the smallest one, sending money by email.
blocks.decision: In March 2000 X.com merged with its neighbour and rival Confinity, which owned a payment product called PayPal. Two companies burning cash to win the same users decided to join forces. The combined company later dropped the X.com name and became PayPal.
blocks.howStarted: X.com was incorporated in March 1999. Confinity had been set up in California in December 1998. PayPal's filings date the merger to 30 March 2000, and Sequoia Capital's Michael Moritz had joined the board in August 1999.
blocks.funding: Musk funded the start of X.com with his own Zip2 money, then raised venture capital. PayPal's 2001 annual report shows he bought later rounds himself too, paying $2.75 a share for Series C and $3.00 for Series D preferred stock.
blocks.whatHappened: Musk was replaced as CEO twice. He ran X.com from March to December 1999, and PayPal from May to September 2000. Peter Thiel took over in September 2000. Even so, Musk stayed on the board and stayed the largest individual shareholder: 11.72% in PayPal's 2002 filing. By the end of 2001, PayPal had 12.8 million accounts. It went public in February 2002, and eBay bought it later that year for about $1.5 billion in stock.
blocks.lesson: Being pushed out as CEO is not the end of your story if you still own the shares. Musk lost the job but kept the stake, and the stake paid for everything that came next.

blocks.name: The Mars mission and the Russian rocket hunt
blocks.idea: Musk's first space idea was not a rocket company. It was a small, privately paid mission to Mars carrying a life-support experiment.
blocks.decision: To do it, he needed a cheap rocket. A Boeing Delta would have cost about $50 million, which he called unpalatable. So he went shopping for second-hand Russian missiles instead. When the deal fell through, he made the decision that defined his life: build the rocket himself.
blocks.howStarted: In 2001 he went to Paris and then to Russia with his friend Adeo Ressi and the aerospace consultant Jim Cantrell. Meetings with Russian rocket officials involved a lot of vodka and very little progress. On a later trip, the price demanded went up and the Russians mocked him, according to Cantrell's account to Esquire.
blocks.funding: His own money, from the Zip2 sale and his PayPal shares. No outside investors were involved.
blocks.whatHappened: Musk told Forbes in 2003 that he negotiated a deal but backed out because the risks of dealing with Russian suppliers outweighed the discount. On the flight home, Cantrell said Musk told him he thought they could build a rocket themselves. That idea became SpaceX.
blocks.lesson: A failed purchase can be the best market research you will ever do. Musk learned rockets were overpriced because nobody had rethought how they were built.

blocks.name: SpaceX
blocks.idea: Make getting to space much cheaper by building rockets in-house and, later, landing and reusing them. SpaceX's 2003 pitch was to carry up to half a tonne to orbit for $6 million a flight. A rival rocket, Orbital's Pegasus, cost $20 million.
blocks.decision: Instead of buying engines and parts from old aerospace suppliers, SpaceX made most of its rocket itself. Musk told Forbes the gap was obvious: there was a need for a reliable, low-cost way to get to space. His first rocket, Falcon 1, was deliberately small.
blocks.howStarted: Space Exploration Technologies started in 2002 in El Segundo, California. Its first engineers came from TRW and Boeing. Falcon 1 launched from the Kwajalein Atoll in the Pacific.
blocks.funding: In the first years it was all Musk's money. Forbes said in 2003 he was covering the first $20 million to $40 million of costs alone and had put in tens of millions. A major outside investment came from Founders Fund, run by his old PayPal colleagues, which put in $20 million, announced in August 2008, just after the third launch failed.
blocks.whatHappened: The first three Falcon 1 launches failed, in 2006, 2007 and August 2008. The fourth reached orbit on 28 September 2008, the first privately developed liquid-fuel rocket to do so. In December 2008 NASA gave SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract for 12 cargo flights to the space station. By 2025 SpaceX flew 170 missions in a single year and carried over 80% of all mass sent to orbit worldwide. In June 2026 it went public in the largest IPO in history.
blocks.lesson: Start with the smallest product that can prove your idea. Falcon 1 was tiny, but surviving its failures taught SpaceX how to build Falcon 9.

blocks.text: Three failed launches before the first success. Read this twice.

blocks.name: Tesla
blocks.idea: Prove that an electric car could be fast and desirable, not a slow box. Start with an expensive sports car, the Roadster, then use the profits and lessons to build cheaper cars for more people.
blocks.decision: Musk did not start Tesla. It was formed in 2003, and Martin Eberhard ran it first. Musk chose to back it in 2004 instead of starting his own car company, and became chairman in April 2004. After Eberhard sued him over credit, a 2009 settlement agreed that five people, including both men, count as co-founders. He added the job of product architect in May 2008 and became CEO in October 2008, in the middle of the financial crisis.
blocks.howStarted: Tesla began in Silicon Valley, not Detroit. For years it ran on a tiny scale: by the end of 2009 it had sold just 937 Roadsters in 18 countries and had 514 employees. From August 2009 it even paid SpaceX about $11,000 a month for building space and IT services at SpaceX's site in Hawthorne.
blocks.funding: Musk's trust bought into round after round, including 40.8 million shares in the 2009 Series E. In late 2008 existing investors lent Tesla $40 million in convertible notes. In 2009 Daimler bought a stake of nearly 10% for about $50 million. In January 2010 Tesla closed a $465 million US government loan.
blocks.whatHappened: Tesla lost $82.8 million in 2008 and $236.4 million in total by September 2009. It went public in June 2010, repaid the government loan in 2013, survived a near-collapse during Model 3 production in 2018, and in 2020 became the world's most valuable carmaker. In 2025 it sold about 1.64 million cars, its second yearly decline in a row, and China's BYD passed it in pure electric sales.
blocks.lesson: You do not have to be the founder to be the builder. Musk joined as an investor, took control when the company was near death, and made it his life's work.

blocks.text: For example: in 2009 and 2010 Tesla's filing shows Musk's salary set at $33,280, the California minimum for executives. But it also says he accepted only $1 a year of it.

blocks.name: SolarCity
blocks.idea: Make solar panels affordable by installing them on homes with little or no upfront cost, and letting customers pay over time.
blocks.decision: On a 2004 road trip to the Burning Man festival, Musk told his cousin Lyndon Rive to get into solar. Lyndon and his brother Peter ran the company, and Musk became its founding chairman instead of the CEO.
blocks.howStarted: SolarCity was founded in 2006. Musk had been chairman since July 2006, according to Tesla's 2010 filing.
blocks.funding: Musk backed it with his own money. Rolling Stone reported that he put $10 million of his PayPal money into SolarCity.
blocks.whatHappened: In 2016 Tesla bought SolarCity for about $2.6 billion. Some Tesla shareholders sued, saying Musk pushed Tesla to rescue a struggling company he had a big stake in. Tesla's other directors settled for $60 million in 2020. Musk fought the case and won in 2022, and in June 2023 the Delaware Supreme Court upheld that the price was fair.
blocks.lesson: When one company you control buys another company you control, expect to defend it in court. Keep records that show the deal was fair.

blocks.name: Hyperloop
blocks.idea: A sealed low-pressure tube in which pods would carry passengers between Los Angeles and San Francisco in about 35 minutes.
blocks.decision: Musk chose not to build it himself. He published the design as an open 'alpha' white paper in August 2013 and invited others to develop it.
blocks.howStarted: It started as a document, not a company: a public paper released in August 2013.
blocks.funding: Musk formed no company to build it. The paper estimated a cost of about $6 billion for a passenger-only version.
blocks.whatHappened: Musk never built it himself. Critics, including economists, said the $6 billion estimate was far too low. His later tunnel company focused on cars in tunnels instead.
blocks.lesson: An open idea gets attention, but without an owner who is responsible for it, it rarely gets built.

blocks.name: OpenAI
blocks.idea: A non-profit lab to develop advanced AI safely and share the benefits, as a counterweight to Google.
blocks.decision: Musk co-founded it in December 2015 with Sam Altman and others, backed by a $1 billion pledge from a group of donors. In early 2018 he said the lab had fallen behind Google and proposed taking control and running it himself. The other founders said no.
blocks.howStarted: OpenAI began in San Francisco as a non-profit research lab.
blocks.funding: Donations from Musk and others. How much Musk actually gave is disputed: Al Jazeera put his early investment at $38 million, while Semafor reported about $100 million.
blocks.whatHappened: Musk left OpenAI's board in February 2018. He later sued it, saying it had abandoned its non-profit mission. On 18 May 2026 a federal jury in Oakland ruled against him, finding his claims were filed too late. Musk said he would appeal.
blocks.lesson: Co-founding is not control. Agree in writing who decides what before you invest money and reputation.

blocks.name: Neuralink
blocks.idea: A small implant that lets the brain talk directly to computers, first to help people with paralysis.
blocks.decision: Musk launched it publicly in 2017, arguing humans needed a faster link to machines as AI improved.
blocks.howStarted: Neuralink started as a small research company and was announced in March 2017.
blocks.funding: Private funding rounds. In June 2025 it closed a $650 million round from investors including ARK Invest, Founders Fund, Sequoia Capital and Thrive Capital; Semafor reported a $9 billion valuation before the new money.
blocks.whatHappened: By June 2025 Neuralink said five people with severe paralysis had received its implant.
blocks.lesson: Deep-tech companies take years before revenue. You need investors who understand that timeline.

blocks.name: The Boring Company
blocks.idea: Dig cheaper, faster tunnels so traffic can move underground.
blocks.decision: Musk started it as a side project and funded it in unusual ways, including merchandise. Most big city projects it announced were later dropped, so it focused on Las Vegas.
blocks.howStarted: It began with test tunnels in the Los Angeles area. In 2018 Chicago picked it to build an express link to O'Hare airport, promising trips of about 12 minutes at no cost to taxpayers.
blocks.funding: Early money came partly from selling hats and a novelty torch called the 'Not-a-Flamethrower' in 2018. In April 2022 it raised $675 million in a round led by Vy Capital and Sequoia Capital, at a $5.675 billion valuation.
blocks.whatHappened: The Los Angeles Westside tunnel plan was dropped in 2018. Chicago's O'Hare express was effectively dead by 2019 after a new mayor said it could not be built without city money. The company built a working loop at the Las Vegas Convention Center instead.
blocks.lesson: Announcing a project is easy. Choose a smaller first project you can actually finish.

blocks.text: Big announcements, small results. Founders, promise less!

blocks.name: Starlink (inside SpaceX)
blocks.idea: Thousands of satellites in low orbit beaming fast internet anywhere on Earth, including villages, ships and planes.
blocks.decision: Instead of selling launches only, SpaceX decided to become its own biggest customer. Its reusable rockets made launching its own satellites cheap.
blocks.howStarted: Starlink was built inside SpaceX, using SpaceX's own rockets.
blocks.funding: Paid for by SpaceX's launch revenue and the money SpaceX raised from investors.
blocks.whatHappened: By 31 March 2026 Starlink had about 10.3 million subscribers, double a year earlier. By 30 September 2026 it had 13.6 million consumer subscribers. In 2025 the Starlink-led Connectivity business brought in about $11.4 billion, most of SpaceX's revenue that year.
blocks.lesson: If your product is expensive for everyone else, find a way to use it yourself first.

blocks.name: Twitter, renamed X
blocks.idea: Buy the world's main public chat platform and run it with fewer rules and far fewer staff.
blocks.decision: Musk first bought a 9.2% stake, then in April 2022 agreed to buy all of Twitter for $54.20 a share, about $44 billion. In July he tried to walk away. Twitter sued to force the deal, and he closed it in October 2022 rather than face trial.
blocks.howStarted: On the day he took over, he fired the CEO, the CFO and the top lawyer.
blocks.funding: About $13 billion of bank loans plus about $33.5 billion of equity promised by Musk, including $7.1 billion from co-investors such as Larry Ellison and Saudi Prince Alwaleed bin Talal.
blocks.whatHappened: One investor, Fidelity, cut the value of its stake by 79% by August 2024. In March 2026 a federal jury found Musk liable for misleading Twitter investors with his tweets during the deal; his lawyers said they would appeal. A year earlier, in March 2025, Musk's AI company xAI had bought X in an all-stock deal valuing it at $33 billion, or $45 billion including debt.
blocks.lesson: Buying a famous brand is not the same as buying a healthy business. Do your homework before you sign, because walking away later is very hard.

blocks.name: xAI
blocks.idea: Build a frontier AI model, Grok, to compete with OpenAI and Google.
blocks.decision: Five years after leaving OpenAI's board, Musk started his own AI lab instead of backing someone else's.
blocks.howStarted: xAI built a giant computer cluster called Colossus inside a former factory in Memphis. Musk said the first 100,000-chip cluster went from start to finish in 122 days.
blocks.funding: Musk's money and then huge outside rounds. In May 2024 it raised $6 billion at a $24 billion valuation from investors including Valor, Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia and Fidelity. In January 2026 Tesla agreed to put about $2 billion into a later round.
blocks.whatHappened: xAI bought X in March 2025. Then, on 2 February 2026, SpaceX bought xAI. Reports valued SpaceX at about $1 trillion and xAI at about $250 billion. Inside SpaceX, xAI's compute business now sells capacity to other AI labs.
blocks.lesson: Speed can be a strategy. Building the hardware fast let a late starter catch up with the leaders.

blocks.name: DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
blocks.idea: Cut US federal spending and staff quickly, using a start-up style team inside the government.
blocks.decision: Musk agreed to lead the effort for the new Trump administration, saying it could save at least $2 trillion.
blocks.howStarted: It began with the new administration in January 2025.
blocks.whatHappened: Musk left at the end of May 2025. DOGE claimed $175 billion in savings, but what it made public added up to less than half of that, and a Reuters review of Treasury data found much smaller spending cuts. Back home, Tesla's deliveries fell about 9% in 2025.
blocks.lesson: Time is a founder's scarcest resource. Every month spent on a side mission is a month your main companies run without you.

blocks.name: America Party
blocks.idea: A new US political party to oppose government overspending.
blocks.decision: Musk announced it on 5 July 2025, after a public fight with President Trump over a spending bill.
blocks.howStarted: Announced through a poll and posts on X.
blocks.whatHappened: By mid-August 2025 the Wall Street Journal reported he had stepped back from the plan to focus on his companies.
blocks.lesson: Not every idea deserves to become a company. Killing one quickly is a skill.

blocks.name: Terafab
blocks.idea: A chip factory shared by Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, to make their own AI chips instead of relying only on suppliers like TSMC, Samsung and Micron.
blocks.decision: Musk argued his companies' demand for chips would soon outrun what suppliers could build.
blocks.howStarted: Announced on 21 March 2026 at an event in Austin, Texas.
blocks.funding: Engadget reported a cost of at least $20 billion, and Fast Company a possible $300 billion price tag.
blocks.whatHappened: It is still early. At the launch event Musk gave no timeline for the factory or its output.
blocks.lesson: When a supplier becomes your bottleneck, consider owning that step yourself, but only when you have the scale.

blocks.text: Musk's first two companies taught him how money really works in start-ups. You can build the product, find the customers and still lose control, because the people who write the cheques get votes. He learned this twice before he turned 30.
Zip2: the merger that fell apart

In spring 1998, Zip2 agreed to merge with CitySearch, its biggest rival in online city guides. On paper it made sense. Together they would have run 175 city guides in 27 of America's top 30 cities, with about 700 staff.

Three weeks into checking each other's books, the deal fell apart. The two companies saw themselves differently. CitySearch thought it was a media company. Zip2 had become more of a software supplier. __A merger that looks good on paper can still fail if the two teams disagree about what the company is.__
...the risk of not seeing eye to eye was too great.
blocks.who: Charles Conn, CitySearch CEO, on the cancelled Zip2 merger (1998)

blocks.text: Less than a year later, Compaq bought Zip2 for ==$307 million in cash==. The company that almost merged with a rival ended up being sold for real money. Musk walked away with about $22 million.
A 'no' to the wrong deal can lead to a better one.
PayPal: losing the job, keeping the shares

X.com was meant to be a full online bank. But the feature people loved most was emailing money. In March 2000, X.com merged with Confinity, the company behind PayPal. That merger is the deal that mattered: two rivals stopped burning cash fighting each other.

Musk ran the combined company from May to September 2000. Then the board replaced him with Peter Thiel. His separation agreement in May 2001 even had a clause about how the company would describe its founders, a sign of how sensitive the question of credit had become.

For example: the separation papers show PayPal bought back some of Musk's shares at exactly the prices he had paid, including Series D stock at $3.00 a share, for $500,000. He kept the rest, and that stake made him the biggest shareholder.

PayPal's biggest rival was not a bank. It was eBay's own payment service, Billpoint. By the end of 2001, about 71% of eBay auctions accepted PayPal, against about 25% for Billpoint. When you are winning on your rival's home ground, the rival may end up buying you. That is what happened.

PayPal went public in February 2002. An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a private company first sells shares to the public on a stock exchange, so anyone can buy them. Its shares jumped 55% on the first day. About eight months later, eBay bought it for about ==$1.5 billion== in stock.

blocks.text: How much did Musk get? His stake was 11.72%. Reports of his payout range from about $165 million to about $180 million, and Rolling Stone calls the $180 million post-tax. Forbes noted in 2003 that he had kept most of the eBay stock he received. That pile of money is what he poured into his next bets, above all SpaceX and Tesla.
Barely 31, rich, and about to risk almost all of it.
In business stories, there is usually one bad year. Musk had one where both of his big companies nearly died in the same few months. It was 2008, the year the global financial crisis hit.
Three strikes at SpaceX

SpaceX's first Falcon 1 launch in March 2006 ended in a fuel leak and fire just after lift-off. The second, in March 2007, climbed 180 miles up, but its second stage began to oscillate and the engine shut down early. The third, in August 2008, failed when an engine timing error made the stages collide during separation.
Just after the third failure, Musk told staff that SpaceX had accepted an outside investment. That was the ==$20 million from Founders Fund==, the venture firm run by his old PayPal colleagues.
It's bad enough to have three strikes. Having four strikes is really kaput.

On 28 September 2008, the fourth Falcon 1 lifted off from a tiny island in the Pacific and reached orbit. It was the first privately built liquid-fuel rocket ever to do that. Three months later, just before Christmas, NASA awarded SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract for 12 cargo flights to the space station.
I just blurted out, 'I love you guys.'
blocks.who: Elon Musk, recalling NASA's call in December 2008 (60 Minutes, 2014)

blocks.text: One contract turned a dying start-up into NASA's partner.
Tesla, the same year

While SpaceX was failing, Tesla was burning cash. Its losses were $78.2 million in 2007 and $82.8 million in 2008. In October 2008, Musk took over as CEO. Reuters reported at the time that its cash balance had dropped to about $9 million.

Tesla's board then approved $40 million of convertible debt from its existing investors, with Musk's trust among them. The notes paid 10% interest. Musk said the amount was significantly more than Tesla needed. VentureBeat said the money was meant to hold the company steady while it waited for a government loan.

Then came the outside help. In May 2009 Daimler, the maker of Mercedes-Benz, bought nearly 10% of Tesla for about $50 million, valuing it at about $550 million after the investment. In January 2010 Tesla closed a ==$465 million loan== from the US Department of Energy to build its Model S factory. __Big partners arrived only after Tesla had survived its worst months.__
That was definitely the worst year of my life.

blocks.text: 2013: the almost-sale to Google

Five years later Tesla was in trouble again. According to Ashlee Vance's biography and his Bloomberg report, in early 2013 Musk began negotiating to sell Tesla to Google through his friend Larry Page, for about $6 billion plus another $5 billion for factories, with Musk staying on as CEO. Tesla and Google declined to comment on it.

After an intense push led by Musk, in May 2013 Tesla reported its first quarterly profit, its stock jumped, and the Google talks ended. That same month Tesla repaid the full government loan, nine years before its original 2022 due date.
He tried to sell Tesla for $6 billion. Remember that number.
2018: production hell and a tweet

Tesla's mass-market Model 3 was supposed to take the company mainstream. Instead, the factory could not build it fast enough. Musk later told Axios that Tesla had been bleeding money like crazy and came within single-digit weeks of death.

In the middle of that, on 7 August 2018, Musk tweeted: "Am considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured." The stock closed up nearly 11% that day. Going private means buying back the shares from public investors, so the company is no longer listed on an exchange.

The SEC, America's stock market regulator, said funding was not secured. It said Musk had never discussed a $420 price with any funder. It also said he worked out $419 as a 20% premium and rounded up partly because of the number's meaning in marijuana culture, which he admitted was not a great reason to pick a price.

Within weeks Musk and Tesla settled. Each paid a ==$20 million== penalty, without admitting or denying the claims. Musk had to step down as Tesla chairman for three years, and Tesla added two independent directors. Shareholders also sued him. In February 2023 a San Francisco jury found him not liable, after about two hours of deliberation.
One tweet cost $40 million. Think before you post.

blocks.text: After surviving, Musk's companies started to grow at a scale few businesses ever reach. This is the part of the story where the fortune was made, mostly on paper, through shares in companies that investors valued very highly.
Tesla goes public

On 29 June 2010, Tesla sold 13.3 million shares at $17 each and raised about ==$226 million==. It priced above the range it had planned, $14 to $16. Reports called it the first American carmaker to go public since Ford in 1956.

At that point Tesla had sold fewer than a thousand cars and had lost money in every quarter since it began. Investors were buying the future, the planned Model S, for which Tesla already had about 2,000 reservations with $5,000 deposits each.
Reservations with deposits are proof people want it.
The SolarCity rescue

In 2016 Tesla bought SolarCity, the solar installer chaired by Musk and run by his cousins, for about $2.6 billion. Critics said Tesla was bailing out a company Musk had a big stake in. Shareholders sued, asking him to return Tesla stock that at one point was worth $13 billion.

Musk won. In 2022 a Delaware judge found Tesla had paid a fair price, and in June 2023 the Delaware Supreme Court upheld the decision, while saying the lower court had made errors in parts of its analysis. __Winning in court is not the same as making a great deal. It only means the deal was not unfair.__
The pay package fights

In 2018 Tesla shareholders approved a pay plan that could give Musk options on about 304 million shares, about 9% of the company, if Tesla hit huge targets. In January 2024 a Delaware judge cancelled it, saying the board was conflicted and shareholders were not told key facts.

Musk then moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas. On 19 December 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court restored the 2018 package, saying cancelling it left Musk unpaid for six years of work. By then it was worth about $139 billion. Musk posted that he was "vindicated."

A month earlier, on 6 November 2025, more than 75% of shareholder votes approved an even bigger plan. It could give Musk up to 423.7 million more Tesla shares over ten years, in 12 blocks. The full payout needs Tesla to be worth $8.5 trillion.

blocks.text: Twitter: the $44 billion detour

In April 2022 Musk agreed to buy Twitter for about $44 billion. Three months later he told Twitter he was ending the deal. Twitter sued. In October 2022 he went ahead at the original price of $54.20 a share, hours before a court deadline, and fired the top executives the same night.

To pay for it, banks lent about $13 billion and Musk promised about $33.5 billion of equity. That included $7.1 billion from co-investors such as Larry Ellison and Saudi Prince Alwaleed bin Talal. The rest had to come from Musk himself, whose wealth was mostly Tesla stock.

By August 2024, Fidelity had cut the value of its X stake by about 79%, which implied X was worth around $9.4 billion. That looked like a huge loss. Then in March 2025 Musk merged X into xAI at $33 billion, and less than a year later folded both into SpaceX.
A bad deal can be rescued by a bigger company you also own.
The AI pivot and the merger of everything

xAI was Musk's answer to OpenAI. It raised money at a pace rarely seen: $6 billion in May 2024 at a $24 billion valuation. Its Colossus supercomputer in Memphis was built, by Musk's count, in 122 days.

On 2 February 2026, SpaceX acquired xAI. Reports valued the combined company at about $1.25 trillion. A merger is when two companies combine into one; here SpaceX paid with its own shares, so xAI's owners became SpaceX owners.

For example: in May 2026 SpaceX signed deals with the AI company Anthropic for computing power on Colossus and Colossus II, about 325,000 Nvidia chips. Anthropic agreed to pay $1.25 billion a month through May 2029.
The biggest IPO in history

SpaceX priced its shares at $135 on 11 June 2026 and started trading on Nasdaq the next day under the ticker SPCX. It raised about ==$75 billion==, the largest IPO ever, about two and a half times Saudi Aramco's record of $29.4 billion. The stock closed its first day up about 19%, at $160.95.

Musk kept control through special Class B shares that carry extra votes and elect a majority of the board. After the IPO he held about 82.4% of the voting power. His pay plan includes 1 billion restricted shares that vest only if SpaceX hits market-value targets and establishes a permanent human colony on Mars with at least one million people.
His bonus literally depends on a million people living on Mars.

Then the market swung. Within days SpaceX's market value peaked at about $2.78 trillion, and Bloomberg's index put Musk's fortune at a peak of about $1.32 trillion, the first ever above $1 trillion. Then one session wiped 16% off SpaceX's shares. By 24 June, after a wider tech sell-off, Musk had dropped back below $1 trillion.

SpaceX kept buying. In June 2026 it borrowed $25 billion through bonds. In August 2026 it completed the purchase of Cursor, the AI coding start-up, paying 389 million SpaceX shares at an implied value of $60 billion.

The business underneath did grow. In the quarter to 30 September 2026, SpaceX's revenue was about $14.6 billion, up from about $5.6 billion a year earlier, and it made a net profit of about $4.4 billion. Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers. __In that quarter, the AI business inside SpaceX brought in more money than rockets and Starlink combined.__

blocks.text: Here is the honest summary. Musk turned about $22 million from his first exit into the first fortune ever to pass $1 trillion, at least on paper, mostly through two decisions: putting nearly everything into SpaceX and Tesla when they looked doomed, and keeping control of both. The same habits, huge bets and bold public promises, also produced Twitter's lost value, the SEC fine, dead tunnel projects and a failed lawsuit against OpenAI.
Copy the courage. Do not copy the tweets.

Picture Tesla's Fremont factory in 2017 and 2018. The company has about a year to reach ==5,000 Model 3 cars a week==. Musk has calculated that number is what keeps Tesla alive. There is no time to build new production lines, so the old ones must simply run faster.

Out of that panic came the rule he now repeats in every company he runs. Musk calls it “the algorithm”. It has five steps, and the order matters: question every requirement, delete any part or process you can, simplify and optimise, speed up the cycle time, and only then automate.

The order is the whole trick. Most engineers start by making a step faster or by giving it to a robot. Musk's point is that __the cheapest, fastest part is the one you deleted__. Optimising something that should not exist is wasted effort, however clever the work looks.
Read the order twice. Delete BEFORE you automate.

For example: at Fremont, Musk first insisted that robots do almost every task from day one. It went badly. He later admitted the big mistake in Nevada and Fremont was trying to automate every step before questioning it, pulled out robots he thought were too slow, and put up an extra assembly line inside a tent in the car park.

Musk also walks the factory floor himself and fixes things he does not like. His biographer Walter Isaacson describes him rewriting the settings of a bolt-fitting machine, telling staff that “Factory settings are always idiotic.” Tesla went on to report record Model 3 output in the second quarter of 2018.
The memo that killed meetings

In April 2018, in the middle of that crunch, Musk sent Tesla staff an email that was first obtained by the websites Electrek and Jalopnik. It read like a rulebook for a company at war. Large meetings should go. Frequent meetings should go unless something is truly urgent. Jargon and made-up acronyms should go.
It is not rude to leave, it is rude to make someone stay and waste their time.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, email to Tesla staff, April 2018

blocks.text: The same email told people to talk to whoever could solve a problem, not to pass messages up and down the chain of command. It said that when a company rule is obviously absurd in a given situation, common sense should win. He also asked the finance team to check every expense worldwide, ==no matter how small==.
Steal this for your first team of five. Today.

Musk's view of where work happens is just as blunt. In June 2022 he emailed Tesla staff that everyone must spend a minimum of 40 hours a week in the office. The office, he added, had to be where your real colleagues sit. When a follower asked about people who think office work is outdated, he replied that they should pretend to work somewhere else.
If you don't show up, we will assume you have resigned.
blocks.who: Elon Musk, email to Tesla staff, June 2022

blocks.text: Surges, couches and 120-hour weeks

Isaacson writes that Musk works in “surges”: bursts of around-the-clock effort on a problem that looks impossible. He expects his teams to surge with him. During the Model 3 crisis, Musk told the New York Times he was working up to ==120 hours a week== and sometimes did not leave the factory for three or four days.

He spent all 24 hours of his 47th birthday at work. Then he flew straight to his brother's wedding, where he was best man, arrived two hours before the ceremony and got back on the plane right after it. He called that year “excruciating”, and the paper said he moved between laughter and tears during the interview.
This is a warning, not a recipe. He nearly broke here.

The habit stuck. After buying Twitter, Musk told the BBC in April 2023 that he sometimes slept on a couch in the company's San Francisco office. The pattern is the same each time: Musk moves into the building where the crisis is and stays until it eases.
How he hires

Musk says he does not care much about degrees. In a 2014 interview with the German magazine Auto Bild, and again when recruiting for Tesla's AI team in 2020, he said a college degree, or even finishing high school, was not required. What he wants is evidence of exceptional ability.

His favourite interview test is simple. At the World Government Summit in Dubai in 2017, he said he asks candidates to describe the hardest problems they worked on and exactly how they solved them. People who really did the work, he explained, know the small details. People who are pretending get stuck after one or two follow-up questions.

For example: if you say you cut a server bill by 40 percent, expect Musk-style follow-ups. Which servers? What did you switch off first? What broke? Who argued with you? A real builder can keep going five levels deep. Someone who watched from the side cannot.
Firing, fast

Musk is equally fast at cutting people. On the day his Twitter purchase closed in October 2022, the chief executive, finance chief and other top executives were out. Within weeks, Twitter staff received an email titled “A Fork in the Road”. It said the new Twitter would need to be ==“extremely hardcore”==, with long hours at high intensity.

Staff had until 5pm the next day to click “yes” on a form. Anyone who did not would leave with three months of severance. By April 2023, Musk said the company had gone from just under 8,000 people to about 1,500, a cut of roughly 80 percent. He said the cuts were “not fun at all”, but claimed the company would otherwise have gone bankrupt.

blocks.text: He took the same style into government. In February 2025, while leading the Department of Government Efficiency, he posted that every federal employee would get an email asking what they had done the week before. Failure to respond, he wrote, would be taken as a resignation. Several agencies told their staff they did not have to reply, and Musk later called it a “very basic pulse check”.
What it is like to work for him

Gwynne Shotwell has run SpaceX's day-to-day business beside Musk for more than two decades. At a TED event in 2018 she said she loves working for him, and that he can be “very aggressive” with timelines in a way that pushes the team to move faster. Former executives quoted by the New York Times in 2026 call her the “Elon whisperer”.
When Elon says something, you have to pause and not immediately blurt out, 'Well, that's impossible.'

She also explained the deal that made the job bearable. Musk's role, she said, is to keep pushing. Her role is to get the company close to comfortable so he can push again. Once she understood that, she said, she started liking her job much more instead of always feeling frustrated.

Not everyone describes it so warmly. Isaacson said Musk can operate “with a real lack of empathy” when staff do not share his sense of urgency, and called him “just brutal” when he tears into someone. In 2022, SpaceX fired employees involved in an open letter criticising Musk's public behaviour. The US labour board later accused SpaceX of firing them illegally. SpaceX went to federal court to try to stop the case, arguing the board's structure was unconstitutional.
Speed is a weapon. Fear is a tax. Know the difference.

Musk's companies look unrelated: cars, rockets, satellites, AI, tunnels, brain chips. Underneath, the same handful of beliefs keeps showing up. Each one has a story behind it, and each story cost him something. Here are the seven that matter most for a young founder.
1. Reason from physics, not from habit

In a 2012 interview with the Digg founder Kevin Rose, Musk took apart a belief everyone held: batteries are expensive and always will be. Historically, he said, battery packs had cost about ==$600 per kilowatt-hour==. So he asked a different question. What are batteries actually made of, and what do those materials cost on the London Metal Exchange?

Cobalt, nickel, aluminium, carbon, some polymers, a steel can. Priced as raw materials, his answer was about ==$80 per kilowatt-hour==. The gap between $600 and $80 was not physics. __The gap was a problem of method, and a problem of method can be solved.__
Boil things down to their fundamental truths and reason up from there, as opposed to reasoning by analogy.

He admits it is tiring. In a 2014 commencement speech at the University of Southern California he said you cannot think this way about everything, because it takes too much mental effort. But for the few decisions that really matter, he called it “a powerful, powerful way of thinking.”
Before you accept a price, ask what it's made of.
2. Try important things even when you will probably fail

Musk did not expect Tesla to survive. In 2014 he told CBS's 60 Minutes, “I thought we would most likely fail.” He started it anyway, because he wanted at least to kill the idea that an electric car had to be ugly, slow and boring like a golf cart.
If something's important enough you should try. Even if you -- the probable outcome is failure.

That belief was tested in 2008. SpaceX's first three Falcon 1 rockets had failed. Musk said a fourth failure would have been “absolutely game over”. He had put the last of his money, about ==$180 million== from the PayPal sale, into Tesla and SpaceX. On the Sunday before Christmas he woke up thinking he had never come closer to a nervous breakdown.
